beats.say: It's called a gambit, but you aren't really giving anything away. It's a loan. If Black takes the pawn, you nearly always get it back.
And the interest is good. Black's d-pawn leaves the middle of the board, and your e-pawn is free to take over.
The ideas are simple, too. Hit d5, press on the knight that guards it, then point your pieces at the king.
We'll build the setup, deal with the five ways Black tries to spoil it, learn the one punch, then watch it land in two games.
Seven moves. Watch the list tick itself off.
Pawn to d4, and Black meets it with d5.
Pawn to c4. That's the gambit. You're offering a pawn to pull Black's d-pawn out of the middle.
Black says no thanks, and guards it with e6. That's the Declined.
Knight to c3 hits d5 again, and Black's knight comes out to guard it.
Bishop to g5 presses on the knight that's holding d5. Black puts the bishop on e7 to back it up.
Now e3, which opens the road for your other bishop. Notice the order: the c1 bishop got out first, so it isn't locked in.
Knight to f3. It looks at e5. Remember that square.
Bishop to d3, aimed straight at h7. That's the setup, and castling comes next.
Now look at what your pieces agree on: d5 in the middle, and h7 by the king. That's the whole plan, in two squares.
Your opponent didn't read the script. Here are the five things they'll try, and you only need one answer to each.
One, and it's the most common under 1800 in our Lichess sample, about three games in ten. Black takes the pawn.
Pawn to e3. Now your bishop is looking at c4, so that pawn's on borrowed time.
About one in four try to hang on to it with b5. It looks logical.
Hit that chain from the side.
About half of them keep holding on.
Trade the pawns, and look what that does. Your rook has a half-open file, and that pawn has left c6.
Queen to f3. The long diagonal runs right to the rook on a8. A piece can block it, but that piece falls instead. The engine says above plus five.
If Black just develops, you simply take it back. Material's level, your centre is better, and the engine says about plus 0.2. The loan is repaid.
Two. The Slav. Black guards with the c-pawn instead, so the light bishop can still get out.

beats.play: Nf3 Nf6 e3 Bf5 Nc3 e6
beats.say: You develop, and out it comes to f5, in front of the pawns. That's the bishop Black was worried about.
So go after it. Knight to h4.
You win the two bishops. It's no knockout, and the engine says about plus 0.3, but it's an edge that lasts.
Three. Knight to f6, which doesn't guard d5 with a pawn at all. That's about one game in six.
So take it. The knight takes back.
Now e4 hits the knight, and you've got both centre pawns for free. The engine says about plus 0.7. You'll see this again in game two.
Four. The bishop comes straight out. It's rare, and it's left something behind.
Queen to b3. That bishop was the only piece guarding b7. About plus 0.7. And if a knight comes to c6, take on d5 first, not on b7.
Five. The Albin Counter-Gambit, Black's own pawn offer. It's rare too, but it comes with a famous trap.
Take the pawn. Black's other pawn jumps to d4 and sits in your way.
Just develop. Knight to f3, then a3, so no bishop can check you on b4. The engine says about plus 0.7, and you're a pawn up.

beats.reset: d4 d5 c4 e5 dxe5 d4
beats.say: Here's the trap. Hit that pawn with e3, and the bishop checks. You block, and the pawn takes on e3.
Grab the bishop, and the pawn takes on f2 with check.
And it takes on g1, turning into a knight with check. Yes, a knight. Grabbing the bishop loses. If you've played e3, retake with the f-pawn. Better still, skip it.

chapters.title: The punch
chapters.from: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6

beats.say: Back to the Declined. One idea works in nearly every line here: settle the centre, then aim at h7.
Take on d5, and Black takes back. The pawns are fixed now, so you know where everything belongs.

beats.play: Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Bd3 Nbd7
beats.say: The same setup as before. Bishop to g5, e3, bishop to d3.
Queen to c2. Queen behind bishop, two pieces on one road to h7.
Only the f6 knight stops them. Your bishop can take that knight whenever it likes, so Black always needs another knight ready to take back.

beats.reset: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 cxd5 exd5 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Bd3 Nbd7 Qc2 c6 Nf3 Re8 O-O Nf8
beats.say: A careful Black brings another guard, knight to f8. Fine. You don't have to break through there.
Switch sides. Rook to b1, then b4 and b5, breaking up Black's queenside pawns. Engine, about plus 0.5. So you always have a plan.

beats.reset: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5
beats.say: Now a warning. This is the Elephant Trap. With the knight on d7, d5 looks free, because the f6 knight seems pinned to the queen.
Take it, and the knight moves anyway, right past that pin.
You take the queen. Then the bishop checks.
Your queen has to block, and it falls. Queens are gone and you've lost a knight for a pawn, about minus five. So check the pin before you trust it.

beats.card: Game one: it goes to plan
beats.say: This game is made up by us and checked by Stockfish. Black's moves are all natural ones.

beats.play: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6
beats.say: The routine. Nothing to think about yet.

beats.play: cxd5 exd5 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O
beats.say: Settle the centre, bishop out, e3.
Bishop to d3, already looking at h7.
And the battery. You've seen this.
Rook to e8 looks active. But that rook was guarding f7, and now only the king does. Remember it.
Your last knight comes out, and Black hits your centre.
You castle. Black gets ready to bring out the other bishop.
Knight to e5, the square you've been looking at. And from there it touches f7.
Black kicks your bishop. It feels strong, and that's the mistake. It takes the engine from about plus 0.5 to about plus two.
Because your bishop isn't going back. It takes on h7, with check.
Black's knight should take it. Then your knight jumps to c6, and the engine still says about plus two. But most kings just step aside, and stay close to home.
King to the corner. The bishop is guarded by your queen, and it covers g8.
Knight takes f7. That's checkmate on move thirteen. The pawn that lost its guard on move eight is the square that finished it.
Also ours, also engine-checked. This time Black answers with reply number three, knight to f6.
No pawn backs up d5. You know what to do.
Take it, the knight takes back, and e4 kicks it.
Back it goes. Your knight comes out to guard e4, and you own the middle. The engine says above plus one.
Develop. Black's bishop comes out and hits your knight.
Bishop to d3, right on the usual road. And Black castles, which feels safe. It's the mistake, because of what comes next.
Now the pawn jumps again, and it kicks the only piece besides the king guarding h7. The engine is already above plus four, whatever Black does.
Knight to d5, the middle of the board, and it hits your knight. But look at the three arrows. There's a very old pattern here.
Bishop takes h7, with check. It's called the Greek gift, because it isn't free. The engine says above plus six.
Black takes it. You've given up a whole bishop.
Knight to g5 with check, and the road for your queen is open.
Going back to g8 is the most stubborn, and queen to h5 then wins Black's queen for the knight. The king can step forward, and that goes badly too.
Most natural of all, into the corner, and away from the knight.
Queen to h5 with check, and the king has to go back.
Checkmate on move twelve. Queen on h7, guarded by the knight. That's the gift's receipt.

chapters.title: Your game plan
chapters.from: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6

beats.card: So how do you win with this?
beats.say: The opening is the easy part. Here's the whole plan in three lines.
One. Hit d5 with the c-pawn and the knight. If Black takes on c4, play e3 and win it back.

beats.play: cxd5 exd5 Bg5 Be7 e3 O-O Bd3 Nbd7
beats.say: Two. Settle the centre, bishop to g5, e3, then bishop to d3, and the road to h7 is open.
Three. Queen to c2 and look for a shot on h7. If Black has it covered, play on the other side with b4 and b5.
That's a good way to win quick games. It isn't a guarantee. A careful opponent gets close to level, and then you have to think.
So do two things next. Drill these lines until your hands know them, then read the Queen's Gambit plan for what to do when the punch doesn't land.
